title: Visiting Goindval
hook: the step-well of Guru Amar Das

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muktsar Sahib, where tradition says the Guru tore up the paper. Your line was the pool of liberation. Did a hello go out to someone you'd drifted from? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

The light changes halfway down. At the top of the stairs it's a bright Punjab afternoon, dust and noise and a river nearby. A few steps lower, the walls close in, the air turns cool, and the sound of the street drops away. Lower still, there's water, dark and still, at the bottom of a deep shaft of stone. People go down barefoot, one step at a time, and some of them are saying something under their breath on every step. This is the baoli, the step-well, at Goindval Sahib.
screen: `BRIGHT AT THE TOP.` → `COOL HALFWAY DOWN.` → `WATER AT THE BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the place. Goindval is a town on the Beas river, and it was the home of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. Tradition says he had the baoli dug there, so that people could reach water in a dry land, and that it became a gathering place for Sikhs. Then the purpose. A step-well is a practical thing. Water sits deep below the ground, so you build stairs down to it. But a Guru's well was never only plumbing. Tradition says the water was open to everyone, whatever their caste, and that openness was itself a teaching. Next, the custom. Some pilgrims recite the Japji Sahib once on every step as they go down, slowly, all the way to the water. It is slow on purpose. Finally, the Guru's word underneath it. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord. The image runs the other way from the baoli: the Japji's stairs go up, the well's stairs go down. And yet both say the same thing about how it's done. Not in a leap. One step, and then the next, and then the next. The baoli at Goindval Sahib still has its stairs, and its water, and its slow walkers.
screen: `A STEP-WELL ON THE BEAS.` · `WATER FOR EVERYONE.` · `THE JAPJI, STEP BY STEP.` · `STAIRS UP, STAIRS DOWN.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk down steps slowly. If there are stairs near you, go to them. If not, take a few slow steps across the room. Put one foot down, and let it land fully before the next. Breathe out on each step. Notice the moment your weight shifts. If you know a line of the Japji, you can say it under your breath, step by step. If not, just count your breaths. Go slower than feels normal. The bell holds the time.
Visiting Goindval. The town of Guru Amar Das on the Beas, and its baoli, where some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step down to the water. Today's word.
Your line: step by step. Today, take one big task and do only the first step of it, slowly and well. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

notes: Japji pauri 32 (Ang 7): 'eit raahi pat pavaReeaa chaReeai hoi ikees' paraphrased as 'along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord'. Please confirm.
The number of steps (tradition says eighty-four) is deliberately not stated (claims rule); the custom is described as 'some pilgrims recite the Japji once on every step'. Please confirm.
'At a time when, in many places, people of different castes were kept away from the same water' is a general historical claim framing the baoli as a teaching; please confirm it is fair.
The langar tradition at Goindval (and Akbar's visit) is deliberately left out to keep one idea.

Editor: cut the unsourced general claim about castes kept from water 'in many places' (now 'tradition says the water was open to everyone, whatever their caste'); cut 'tradition counts the steps', which hinted at an unstated number.
